claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native or mill-scale iron oxide layer remaining from standard processing.
The stability of the native iron oxide layer determines whether corrosion-related degradation of Q235 steel is initiated or suppressed.
At room temperature, the naturally formed oxide layer on Q235 steel is relatively coherent and passive.
At room temperature, the native oxide layer acts as an effective barrier to chloride attack.
Elevated temperature produces thermal expansion and stress that cause microcracking, spallation, or delamination of the oxide layer.
Disruption of the oxide layer exposes fresh Q235 steel to the environment.
Oxide disruption facilitates chloride penetration and accelerates localized corrosion.
The continuity and adhesion of the native oxide layer are the structural mediators controlling the proposed corrosion response.
Q235 specimens exposed to 0.5 M NaCl at approximately 25 degrees Celsius will exhibit low mass loss and low pitting density.
Q235 specimens exposed at approximately 70–90 degrees Celsius will exhibit greater oxide-layer disruption than room-temperature specimens.
Elevated-temperature specimens will have higher corrosion current density, mass loss, pitting density, and pitting intensity than the reference specimens.
Q235 steel stored under ambient, benign conditions with an intact native oxide layer typically has a very low corrosion rate.
The proposed oxide-breakdown mechanism is expected to dominate in oxygenated, chloride-rich aqueous solutions at 70–90 degrees Celsius when the oxide has not undergone complete breakdown.
Very high temperatures or aggressive acids may activate corrosion pathways in addition to oxide breakdown.
Mechanical stress, humidity, and minor compositional variation in the oxide may influence the corrosion behavior.
Potentiodynamic electrochemical testing can provide corrosion-related polarization measurements for the proposed comparison.
